MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is patellar maltracking after TKA?"
- "Patella **off-centre** in the trochlear groove in flexion or extension, resurfaced or not."
- "**Commonest** TKA complication → cause = **component position**, rarely the patella itself."
- "Work-up → **Merchant view** for tilt or subluxation → **CT for component rotation** before soft-tissue surgery."

### Definition & significance
- Maltracking → patella off-centre in the groove, with or without **resurfacing**
- Most common, most **overlooked** TKA (total knee arthroplasty) complication → component position = key answer (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Consequences → **anterior knee pain**, subluxation or dislocation, more wear, fracture risk

### Signs & imaging
- Clinical → apprehension, anterior knee **pain on stairs**
- **Merchant** (skyline) view → lateral **tilt** or **subluxation** of the button
[[FIG: Fig 13.1 · 13.1
- Unexplained maltracking → **CT for component rotation** before any soft-tissue procedure (Miller)
- Femoral rotation on CT → against the surgical TEA (transepicondylar axis), **Berger** method → chapter 12

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Commonest · overlooked · component first · Merchant, then CT**

13.2.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you check tracking on the table?"
- "Trials in, **retinaculum open**, **no hand** on the patella → flex through the **full range**."
- "**No-thumb test** → medial facet stays on the medial condyle, button congruent."
- "Borderline → **single stitch** at the superior pole · **deflate the tourniquet** before any release."

### The tests
- Trials + provisional spacer → does the patella stay in the groove unaided and unclosed?
- **No-thumb test** → knee extended, press the patella down, flex → medial facet lifts off = maltracking
- Hand on the patella = **cheating** → masks maltracking · hand off → it dislocates (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Adequate → button tracks **congruently**, minimal or no lateral pressure, before closure

#### Towel clip & full flexion
- **Towel clip test** → clip the open retinaculum, move the knee → tracks only when held = failed
- Closure hides maltracking · test through **full flexion** → early tracking may fail deep
- Borderline → **single stitch** at the superior pole, then recheck
[[FIG: Fig 13.2 · 13.2

PITFALL — testing with the tourniquet up
- Tourniquet **tethers the quadriceps** → no-thumb test inaccurate, false lateral pull (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Say → "**deflate and re-test before any lateral release**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **No thumb · no closure · full flexion · tourniquet down**

13.3.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is the Q angle and why does it matter?"
- "ASIS → patella centre vs patella centre → **tibial tuberosity** · knee extended, quadriceps relaxed."
- "Bigger angle → bigger **lateral pull** → lateral subluxation of the patella."
- "Every malposition that **raises the Q angle** causes maltracking → restoring it is a TKA goal."

### Definition
- Line ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine) → patella centre vs patella centre → **tibial tuberosity**
[[FIG: Fig 13.3 · 13.3
- Campbell (Hvid) → extended **femoral anatomic axis** vs patella centre–tubercle line
- Measured knee extended, quadriceps relaxed · falls in flexion as the patella seats

PITFALL — which normal Q angle?
- Handbook 10–15° (men 10–13°, women 12–15°) · Prof Abdel Karim 13–18°, women ≈18°
- Say → "**about 15°, women higher** (wider pelvis) · abnormal >15° men, >20° women (Campbell)"

### Restraints
- Quadriceps pull along the femoral axis, except **VMO** (vastus medialis obliquus) → medialises in extension
- **VMO** = dynamic · **MPFL** (medial patellofemoral ligament) = static restraint to lateral shift

#### Why it matters
- Larger Q angle → more **lateral subluxation** force
[[FIG: Fig 13.4 · 13.3
- Tubercle lateral or trochlea medial → enlarges the lateral vector
- Restoring the Q angle = TKA goal, even without resurfacing (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Causes → **patient**, **implant design**, **surgical technique** factors

- **ASIS–patella–tubercle · about 15° · bigger angle = bigger lateral pull**

13.4.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which patient and design factors?"
- "Patient → **residual valgus**, rotational deformity, **patella alta**, trochlear dysplasia, old instability."
- "Design → **patella-friendly** femur: long flange, high lateral wall, groove angle up to **7°**."
- "Design helps, but **cannot rescue an internally rotated** component."

### Patient factors
- Neglected **PF (patellofemoral) arthritis**, pre-existing instability → not causal alone, less margin
- **Trochlear dysplasia**, previous dislocation → predict instability after TKA
- **Residual genu valgum** → Q angle up · valgus **>20°** often with subluxation (Prof Abdel Karim)
[[FIG: Fig 13.5 · 13.4
- Valgus, femoral anteversion, external tibial torsion → valgus force on the patella

#### Valgus & alta
- Valgus → lateral tubercle + tight lateral retinaculum → **lateral release** more often
- Patella first contacts the trochlea at ≈**20°** flexion (Campbell)
- 0–20° → **MPFL + VMO** hold it · from 30° → bony or prosthetic trochlea centres it
- **Patella alta** → delayed trochlear entry → longer unprotected range → instability

### Implant design
- Older **patella-unfriendly** designs, short anterior flange → more patellar complications
- **Patella-friendly** → longer flange, higher lateral flange, continuous anterior **radius of curvature**
- Earlier capture in flexion · raised lateral wall = native buttress
- Built-in **trochlear groove angle** up to **7°** → better tracking (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 13.6 · 13.4

#### Limits of design
- Trochlea + femoral rotation + patellar thickness + joint line → fewer **lateral releases**
- **Selective resurfacing** → native patella in an anatomic groove ≈ resurfaced TKA
- **Dome** buttons tolerate rotational mismatch · anatomic buttons need exact orientation
- Design **cannot rescue** an internally rotated component

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Valgus · alta · dysplasia · friendly flange · 7° groove · rotation beats design**

13.5.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do femoral and tibial errors cause maltracking?"
- "**Femur internally rotated or medialised** → trochlea medial → patella relatively lateral."
- "**Tibia internally rotated or medialised** → tubercle relatively lateral → Q angle up."
- "Aim → femur **slight ER**, central or lateral · tray on the **medial third** of the tubercle (axes → chapter 10)."

### Femoral rotation
- **Internal rotation** (IR) → trochlea medial → patella **subluxes laterally** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 13.7–13.8 · 13.5
- Flexion-gap shape and the hypoplastic condyle → 10 Technique

### Femoral position & size
- **Medialised** femur → trochlea medial to the tubercle → Q angle up (Miller)
- Keep it **central** · between sizes → **lateralise**, cover the lateral condyle (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **Flexed** → flange lifted, patella impinges · **extended** → overstuffed, anterior pain, less flexion
- **Oversized** → trochlea too anterior → instability or limited flexion

### Tibial component
- Tray IR = relative **ER of the tubercle** → tubercle lateral → Q angle up (Prof Abdel Karim)
[[FIG: Fig 13.9 · 13.5
- Tray IR → also unexplained **pain and stiffness**
- **Medialised** tray → articulation medial to the tubercle → Q angle up (Miller)
- Combined femoral + tibial IR → maltracking, more pain, worse complications (Campbell)

#### Setting tray rotation
- Rotation **central or external**, never internal · lateralise on the lateral cortex
- Tray over the **medial third** of the tubercle (Miller) · other landmarks → 10 Technique
[[FIG: Fig 13.10 · 13.5

13.6.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where do you place the patellar button?"
- "**Medial**, slightly superior, never lateral or inferior → recreates the median eminence."
- "Medial button → Q angle down · lateral button → Q angle up → lateral subluxation."
- "Cut facets to **equal thickness** (lateral cut shallower), restore **thickness** → no tilt, no overstuffing."

### Mediolateral position
- Button always **medial**, never lateral → medial lowers, lateral raises the Q angle (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 13.11 · 13.6
- Patella = the only component placed **medial** → counters the valgus force
- Medialise to the **median eminence**, not the centre of the available bone (Campbell)
- Proper position ≈**2–3 mm** medialised (Handbook)

#### Central or lateral button
- Centralised button → patella must track with a **higher Q angle**
- Lateral button → no median eminence → lateral subluxation in extension
- Medial button leaves lateral bone → uncovered bone impinges → **lateral facetectomy**

- Symmetric posterior cut on asymmetric facets → **tilt** · equal facet thickness → flat button
- **Lateral facet** cut is often much shallower than the medial (Campbell)

- Height central, may be superior, **never inferior** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Proximal overhang of the button → **patellar clunk syndrome** (Campbell)

13.8.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you manage maltracking?"
- "On the table → **deflate the tourniquet** first → partial, then complete **lateral release**."
- "Then resurfacing → **reposition the malpositioned component** → never release over malrotation."
- "Late → physiotherapy → CT → **revise the component** · distal realignment only with extreme caution."

### Intraoperative ladder
- **Tourniquet deflation** first → cheapest step, false problem before real one
- Deflation spared release in **31%** · **48%** reverted to normal in another study (Campbell)

| Step after deflation | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Partial lateral release |
| 2 | Complete lateral release |
| 3 | Patellar resurfacing → even without prior PF arthritis |
| 4 | Reposition the malpositioned component |

### Lateral release
- Tracks poorly only in flexion → standard **lateral release**, muscle not cut (Prof Shokry)
- **Pie-crusting** first → responds = done · else incision extended, left unsutured
- Done **inside out**, sparing the **superior lateral genicular artery**
[[FIG: Fig 13.15 · 13.8
- Risk → patellar **AVN** (avascular necrosis) and fracture, worse after medial parapatellar arthrotomy (Campbell)

### After surgery
- Components well placed → release (rarely enough alone) → **proximal realignment**
- Malposition → inspect and **revise** the component · isolated release over malrotation fails
- **Distal realignment** (tibial tubercle osteotomy) → extreme caution → nonunion = serious loss (Campbell)

#### Button & rehabilitation
- Button placed **medially and superiorly** → solves dislocation or rotation problems (Prof Shokry)
- Late maltracking → strengthening, physiotherapy → failure → re-exploration ± button

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Deflate · release · resurface · reposition · revise**
